sections.h: The Epistle of Enoch (1 Enoch 91–108)
sections.b: The last part of 1 Enoch is a letter in Enoch's name to "all my children who live on the earth" (92:1). It opens with Enoch's farewell to his family (91:1–10), includes the Apocalypse of Weeks (93:1–10 with 91:11–17), and then delivers about thirty woes against the rich and unjust (94–100), a debate about death and reward (102–104) and a short word of the Lord (105). Chapters 106–107 tell of Noah's birth, and chapter 108 is a late appendix. The Greek papyrus of 97:6–107:3 calls it the Epistle of Enoch. Most scholars date the core to the 100s BC in Judea.

common: The Epistle of Enoch was written to comfort poor and persecuted Jews and warn their rich oppressors.
uncommon: Some scholars think chapters 92–105 once circulated on their own, before chapter 91 was added in front and 106–108 at the end.

sections.h: The paths of righteousness and of violence in 1 Enoch
sections.b: The Epistle of Enoch is built on two kinds of paths. Enoch urges his children to walk in "the paths of righteousness" and not in "the paths of violence," for those who walk in injustice will perish forever (91:18–19). The faithful are to choose righteousness and "a life worth choosing" and walk in the paths of peace (94:3–4); the blessed walk in the path of righteousness (99:10). This is one of the fullest Jewish forms of the two-ways teaching before Jesus' narrow and wide roads (Matthew 7:13–14).

sections.h: Woes on the rich in 1 Enoch
sections.b: No Jewish writing before Jesus attacks the rich more sharply than the Epistle of Enoch. "Woe to you rich! You have trusted in your wealth" (94:8). The rich build houses with others' labor (99:13), boast of full storerooms (97:8–9), dress in purple (98:2) and look righteous only because they are wealthy (96:4). Their wealth will run away like water (97:10). George Nickelsburg showed how close this is to Luke's Gospel: the woes on the rich (Luke 6:24), the rich fool (Luke 12:16–21) and the rich man and Lazarus (Luke 16:19–31). James 5:1–6 reads almost like a summary.

common: The Epistle's woes on the rich are close in idea to Jesus' teaching in Luke.
uncommon: A few scholars have argued that Luke knew the Epistle of Enoch directly; most think both draw on shared Jewish tradition.

sections.h: The cry of the poor in 1 Enoch 103
sections.b: 1 Enoch 103:9–15 gives the lament of the suffering righteous in their own words: they toiled and had no control over their labor, became "the tail" instead of "the head" (Deuteronomy 28:13), were robbed and killed, and complained to the rulers, who helped the robbers and hid the murders. Enoch answers that heaven remembers them and that they will shine like the lights of heaven (104:1–2). It is a rare picture of oppression seen from below in the time between the Testaments.

sections.h: Life after death in the Epistle of Enoch
sections.b: The Epistle is among the earliest Jewish writings to teach plainly that the righteous are rewarded after death. "The righteous will rise from their sleep" (91:10; 92:3). The souls of the righteous dead are told not to fear: good things are written down for them, their spirits will live and rejoice (102:4–103:4), and they will shine like the lights of heaven and be companions of the angels (104:2–6). This answers the sinners who say that all die alike (102:6–8), an argument that echoes Ecclesiastes 9:2. Daniel 12:2–3 and Wisdom of Solomon 3–5 share the same hope.

claude.title: Claude's observation: a debate inside the Bible's own wisdom
claude.body: This is my own reading. The sinners of 102:6–8 do not speak like pagans; they speak like Ecclesiastes. That suggests the Epistle was not only fighting rich oppressors but arguing with a Jewish view, found in the Bible itself, that death makes everyone equal. Enoch's answer does not reject Ecclesiastes' observations but adds what Ecclesiastes leaves open: what happens to the spirit after death. Scholars such as Nickelsburg note the parallel with Wisdom of Solomon 2; I am going a step further in reading the Epistle as an answer to the questions Ecclesiastes raises.

sections.h: Sheol in the Epistle of Enoch
sections.b: In the Epistle, Sheol is no longer the same for all. The righteous went down to Sheol in grief (102:5; 102:11), but their spirits will live and rejoice (103:4). The sinners' souls are brought down to Sheol to be miserable, into darkness, chains and burning flame (103:7–8), and some will be "killed in Sheol" (99:11). This is a step between the Hebrew Bible's shadowy Sheol and the New Testament's Hades and Gehenna (Luke 16:23).

sections.h: Heavenly books in 1 Enoch 91–108
sections.b: Heaven writes everything down in the Epistle. The world is "written down for destruction" (91:14); every sin is written in heaven every day (98:7–8; 104:7); the words of the sinners are read out before the Holy Great One (97:6). The names of the righteous are written before the Great One (104:1), while sinners' names are wiped out of the holy books (108:3). Enoch also reads the heavenly tablets (93:2; 103:2; 106:19). The pictures match Exodus 32:32–33, Daniel 7:10 and Revelation 20:12.

sections.h: The Ten Weeks of 1 Enoch
sections.b: The Apocalypse of Weeks (93:1–10; 91:11–17) divides all history into ten weeks. Enoch is born seventh in the first week (93:3). Seven weeks run from creation to the writer's own day; three more bring the righteous sword, the world's judgment and a new heaven that shines sevenfold (91:16). Daniel 9:24–27 counts seventy weeks; both books use the number seven to show that history follows God's plan.

sections.h: The chosen plant and Noah the remnant
sections.b: The Ten Weeks trace a "plant of righteousness" from Abraham (93:5) to "chosen righteous ones" picked out of it at the end of the seventh week (93:10). The Noah story calls Noah a "remnant" who will be left on the earth (106:16–18). Both say that God saves a righteous few through judgment, like the remnant of Isaiah 10:20–22.

sections.h: The birth of Noah in 1 Enoch
sections.b: 1 Enoch 106–107 tells how Noah was born white as snow and red as a rose, with eyes like the sun, and spoke with God at birth. Lamech feared the child was a Watcher's son; Enoch assured Methuselah that he was truly Lamech's son and the one who would survive the Flood with his three sons. The name Noah is explained as "remnant" (106:18) and as "he will bring joy to the earth" (107:3; compare Genesis 5:29). The Aramaic Genesis Apocryphon (1Q20) tells the same story.

sections.h: The Flood as the first judgment in 1 Enoch 91–107
sections.b: The Epistle treats the Flood as the first world judgment and a model of the last. Violence grows and a great punishment comes, then injustice grows a second time before the final judgment (91:5–9). In the Ten Weeks, the second week brings "the first end" and a man saved (93:4). Enoch tells Methuselah the Flood will last one year and wash the earth clean (106:15–17). Jesus and 2 Peter use the same pattern (Matthew 24:37–39; 2 Peter 3:5–7).

sections.h: The Watchers in the Epistle and the Noah story
sections.b: The Epistle mentions the Watchers rarely but at key points. In the tenth week the eternal judgment falls on the Watchers (91:15). Enoch tells Methuselah that in the days of Jared some from heaven broke the Lord's word, married women and fathered beings of flesh (106:13–17). Yet the Epistle also insists that people made sin themselves; it was not sent from heaven (98:4).

sections.h: Idols and demons in 1 Enoch 99
sections.b: 1 Enoch 99:7–9 condemns those who worship stones, carve images of gold, silver, wood and clay, and worship unclean spirits and demons: they will get no help. The list is very close to Revelation 9:20 and draws on Deuteronomy 32:17 and Psalm 115:4–8.

sections.h: A new heaven in the tenth week
sections.b: At the end of the Ten Weeks, "the first heaven will depart and pass away, and a new heaven will appear," and the powers of heaven will shine sevenfold forever (91:16). Then come weeks without number, in which sin will not even be mentioned (91:17). Revelation 21:1 and 2 Peter 3:13 share the hope, probably both drawing on Isaiah 65:17.

sections.h: How the Epistle of Enoch survived
sections.b: The Epistle survives whole only in Ge'ez. The Aramaic 4Q212 (first century BC) preserves parts of 91–94 and shows that 91:11–17 originally followed 93:10. 4Q204 preserves parts of 104–107; J. T. Milik (1976) restores the two verses of chapter 105 in it, though he thought the words "I and my son" were not there. A Greek papyrus of the 300s AD (Chester Beatty–Michigan, published by Campbell Bonner in 1937) covers 97:6–107:3, lacks chapter 105 and ends with the title "Epistle of Enoch." A Coptic fragment of 93:3–8 is reported, and a Latin excerpt of chapter 106 survives (found by M. R. James, 1893). Chapter 108 is known only in Ge'ez. The Epistle itself foresees its words written "in their own languages" (104:11).

sections.h: Enoch's claim about his own books
sections.b: 1 Enoch 104:10–13 warns that sinners will change Enoch's words and write books of their own, and promises that his true books will be given to the righteous and the wise. Woes fall on those who write lying words (98:15). The Ethiopian Orthodox Church sees these books given to it in its Bible; other churches note that a book's claim about itself does not make it Scripture.

sections.h: Persecuted righteous in 1 Enoch
sections.b: The Epistle speaks of the righteous hunted down (95:7), tormented and burned with fire (100:7), robbed and murdered while the rulers hid it (103:15). Chapter 108 honors those who loved God more than gold and gave their bodies to torment, and promises each a throne of honor (108:7–12).

sections.h: Prayer as a case in heaven's court
sections.b: In the Epistle, the prayer of the righteous is a legal appeal. The sinners will hear it on the day of judgment (97:3); it reaches the Lord (97:5); the righteous lay their prayers before the angels as a witness (99:3) and keep crying out for justice (104:3). Compare the widow and the judge in Luke 18:1–8 and the martyrs' cry in Revelation 6:9–10.

sections.h: Angels who bring the record before God
sections.b: 1 Enoch 99:3 tells the righteous to set their prayers before the angels, so that the angels can lay the sinners' sin before the Most High. The angels also remember the righteous for good before the Great One (104:1). Tobit 12:12 and Revelation 8:3–4 share the picture of angels presenting prayers.

sections.h: Reward and punishment after death in the Epistle
sections.b: The Epistle keeps the Bible's principle that people are repaid for their deeds (95:5; 100:7), but moves the payment beyond death. The rich die in honor (103:5–6) and the righteous die in misery (102:5), yet the true reward is the share of the righteous dead, "far greater than the share of the living" (103:3). Psalm 73:17 and Luke 16:25 make the same turn.

sections.h: Courts that failed the poor
sections.b: The righteous of 103:14–15 complained to the rulers, who would not listen and helped their oppressors. The sinners "pass judgment on the righteous" (100:10), lay curses (95:4) and give false testimony (95:6). Enoch moves the case to heaven's court, where every deed is read out (97:6).

sections.h: The fiery chaos of 1 Enoch 108
sections.b: 1 Enoch 108:3–6 describes the place where the spirits of sinners are thrown: a shapeless wilderness with no earth, a deep cloud, a blazing fire and the sound of weeping. 103:8 speaks of darkness, chains and burning flame. The New Testament speaks of Gehenna, the lake of fire and weeping and grinding of teeth (Matthew 13:42; Revelation 20:14–15).

sections.h: "I and my son" (1 Enoch 105:2)
sections.b: In 105:2 the Lord says, "I and my son will be united with them forever." Christian readers, including Ethiopian Orthodox teachers, hear the Father and the Son (John 14:23). The chapter is missing in the Greek papyrus but seems to have been in the Aramaic 4Q204. J. T. Milik, who restored that fragment, judged the gap too short for "I and my son" and called the phrase a Christian gloss (1976). Others read it as Jewish usage (compare 4 Ezra 7:28, "my son the Messiah").
